visuals.anchor: The mechanism: turn distance into size
visuals.title: Why distance becomes size
visuals.alt_text: A side elevation shows equally tall performers at different distances from one camera. The inset illustrates the change in projected size; framing and set dressing must conceal the depth separation.
visuals.caption: Equal-height performers look different sizes because one is farther away. Scenery and framing must hide that separation. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Replace the mirror with an opening into a second, reversed set. Put another performer on the other side, and choreograph the two performances to resemble a person and their reflection.
visuals.title: Where the reflection’s room really is
visuals.alt_text: An oblique cutaway reveals an open frame between two reversed physical rooms. Two matched performers supply the apparent reflection; there is no mirror glass.
visuals.caption: The camera sees a second performer through an empty frame. Matched rooms and gestures supply the reflection the audience expects. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The mechanism: change perspective, preserve framing
visuals.title: Keep the face, change the space
visuals.alt_text: Two invented frames hold the subject at the same size while the background scale changes. Camera distance and focal length change together.
visuals.caption: Moving the camera changes depth relationships. An opposing zoom keeps the person the same size while the background changes. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The opening puzzle: how does the vase repair itself?
visuals.title: Change the order, change the event
visuals.alt_text: A vase breaks across recorded frames. Reversing their order makes the same fragments appear to reassemble; it does not reverse physical time on set.
visuals.caption: The same fragment paths become reassembly when their recorded order is reversed. No piece needs to find a new route. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Four recurring ways to hide the join
visuals.title: Hide the change under an obstruction
visuals.alt_text: A foreground obstruction conceals the change from one take to another. Position and motion must agree as the picture becomes visible again.
visuals.caption: Join the takes while the foreground blocks the view. The position and movement revealed afterward must still agree. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Why rotating the camera alone is different
visuals.title: Move the room while gravity stays fixed
visuals.alt_text: The room turns while gravity remains vertical. The performer’s contact with its surfaces and the camera relationship determine the apparent change in gravity.
visuals.caption: Gravity continues to pull down in the studio. The turning room and camera make a different surface look like the floor. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: One fictional object can be represented by several physical versions, each built for a different job.
visuals.title: Three versions, one screen object
visuals.alt_text: Appearance, action and aftermath can use different versions of a prop. The drawing illustrates continuity across versions without specifying construction or stunt procedures.
visuals.caption: Handling, breaking and aftermath can use matched versions of one fictional object. Its recognizable appearance connects the shots. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: A slide projector inside the computer
visuals.title: A picture projected onto simplified geometry
visuals.alt_text: An image projects onto simplified geometry. A limited camera change can reveal depth, but missing surfaces and stretched imagery restrict how far the new view can travel.
visuals.caption: The projection camera places the picture on geometry; the viewing camera sees the resulting depth. A large move can expose missing surfaces. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The disappearance is a lighting cue
visuals.title: Follow the reflection
visuals.alt_text: A partly reflective sheet sends light from a hidden subject toward the camera while transmitting the visible set. The two contributions overlap in the viewed image.
visuals.caption: The glass adds a hidden performer’s reflection to the visible room. Reducing the hidden light makes the apparition fade. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The second puzzle: why isn’t the enormous building transparent?
visuals.title: Choose which area reflects
visuals.alt_text: Reflective regions supply the model view; a cleared patch admits live action behind the mirror. The camera, mirror and two sources must align in the final image.
visuals.caption: The mirror supplies reflected scenery; the cleared patch supplies live action. Align their edges to make one continuous place. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: How the optical version works
visuals.title: Accumulate light inside one frame
visuals.alt_text: Three instants contribute light to a single open exposure. The accumulated first frame and a slightly changed second frame form successive animation images.
visuals.caption: Several moments of light accumulate inside one exposed frame. Changing the arrangement for the next frame builds the apparent journey. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Three effects to separate
visuals.title: A sharp core and a soft halo
visuals.alt_text: The drawn bright core stays localized while scattered light extends its influence. The rings indicate a halo schematically, rather than a calibrated filter response.
visuals.caption: Some light remains in a defined bright core while some spreads around it. The rings indicate spread, not a measured filter response. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: How the trick works
visuals.title: Remove the replacement interval
visuals.alt_text: Recording stops while an object is replaced. Joining the before and after segments omits the replacement interval and creates an immediate screen change.
visuals.caption: The replacement happens between the moments the audience sees. Matching the surrounding scene makes the change appear instantaneous. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Two controls make the effect flexible
visuals.title: Separate viewpoint from event time
visuals.alt_text: Several physical cameras surround one performer. A timing strip distinguishes simultaneous exposures from staggered exposures before their viewpoints are sequenced.
visuals.caption: Several cameras record different viewpoints. Simultaneous exposures hold one instant; staggered exposures let the action advance. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.article_title: Motion Control and Repeatable Camera Movements
visuals.anchor: The opening puzzle: how can one actor appear twice while the camera keeps moving?
visuals.title: Match the move, combine the passes
visuals.alt_text: Two passes record one actor in different places while the same camera repeats a straight path and timing. Dashed camera symbols mark earlier positions. Matching frames combine both roles.
visuals.caption: One camera repeats the same timed move for separate passes. Combine corresponding frames so the elements share a viewpoint. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The opening puzzle: why does running the camera faster make the action slower?
visuals.title: Count frames, then count screen seconds
visuals.alt_text: One second captured at 12, 24 or 48 frames per second lasts 0.5, 1 or 2 seconds when played at 24 frames per second. Bar lengths represent screen duration.
visuals.caption: At 24-frame playback, 48 captured frames fill two seconds and 12 fill half a second. These bars describe duration, not exposure. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The effect has three jobs: anticipation, event, and aftermath
visuals.title: Coordinate evidence and consequence
visuals.alt_text: Performance, a visible surface cue and sound are timed around one apparent impact. Their agreement creates the event; this is a timing diagram, not a practical-effects rig.
visuals.caption: The visible disturbance, reaction and sound meet around one apparent impact. Their agreement supplies the event’s weight. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The opening puzzle: how can a punch land when it misses?
visuals.title: Hide the gap in the chosen view
visuals.alt_text: An overhead plan separates an apparent strike from the other performer along the camera viewing direction. The inset shows how their projected shapes overlap; angle, reaction and timing imply contact.
visuals.caption: From this camera angle, fist and face overlap in the picture while remaining apart in space. A timed reaction and sound complete the hit. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The puzzle: why bring an enormous black sheet to a brightly lit film set?
visuals.title: Remove a contribution, retain the key
visuals.alt_text: An overhead lighting plan shows the main light reaching the subject from one side. A matte black flag on the other side intercepts returning light before it reaches the subject.
visuals.caption: Keep the main light while intercepting illumination returning from the other side. The shadow side darkens because it receives less light. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The principle: shrink the world, then photograph it from inside that world
visuals.title: Build the composite from parts
visuals.alt_text: A low camera photographs a model building on a stage. Viewpoint and lighting suggest full scale; atmosphere and added figures can complete the image. The simplified geometry is not a measured miniature setup.
visuals.caption: A low viewpoint makes the model feel like a world around the camera. Lighting, focus and added elements must support that apparent scale. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: A film example: the rowing race in *The Social Network*
visuals.title: Assign sharpness by depth
visuals.alt_text: An invented flat scene has a readable middle-depth band and softer near and far regions. The gray regions denote softness; they are not literal blur filters or a universal image-height mask.
visuals.caption: Blur should follow scene depth. A fixed horizontal strip can fail when buildings or overlapping objects cross several distances. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The puzzle: where is the camera standing?
visuals.title: Open the set for the camera
visuals.alt_text: An exploded cutaway shows a wall panel lifted away from a room. A camera outside the open side photographs the interior while framing conceals the missing wall.
visuals.caption: The camera looks through a removed wall. The remaining room and the frame boundaries preserve the appearance of enclosure. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The puzzle: how many houses make one Pemberley?
visuals.title: One estate, two real houses
visuals.alt_text: An edit connects an exterior from one place with an interior from another. These generic buildings explain screen geography without depicting an actual estate or implying a documented shot order.
visuals.caption: Matching action and visual details connect an exterior and interior filmed elsewhere. The edit establishes their fictional adjacency. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: How the trick works
visuals.title: Two regions, two focus distances
visuals.alt_text: A partial close-up attachment supplies nearer focus in one image region while the uncovered region uses the main lens’s farther focus. Intermediate distances can remain soft.
visuals.caption: The attachment focuses one region nearer while the main lens focuses the other farther away. Conceal the transition; intervening space can remain soft. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Probe, periscope and snorkel: the useful distinction
visuals.title: Separate the viewpoint from the camera body
visuals.alt_text: A straight probe and a right-angle optical head move the viewpoint away from the camera body. Green shows the conceptual viewing path, not a complete lens prescription.
visuals.caption: Only the small optical head must reach the desired viewpoint. The recording camera can stay outside the confined space. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The puzzle: why isn’t the person moving with the background?
visuals.title: Make the torso the reference frame
visuals.alt_text: A body mount keeps the torso comparatively stable within the frame; a room camera lets the performer move against a steadier environment. Real heads and limbs can still move independently.
visuals.caption: A body mount travels with the torso, so the surroundings shift around it. A room-supported camera anchors a different reference. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: What the laboratory does
visuals.title: Retain the silver image
visuals.alt_text: A normal path removes silver after color development; a retention process leaves some silver with the dyes. The diagram separates processing choices without prescribing laboratory chemistry.
visuals.caption: Normal processing removes the image silver. Retaining some alongside the dyes changes tonal contrast and color reproduction. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The opening puzzle: where did the animator’s hands go?
visuals.title: Build motion between exposures
visuals.alt_text: A puppet’s pose changes between individual recorded exposures. Joints can move and parts can be replaced; the finished sequence contains the photographed states, not the animator’s interventions.
visuals.caption: The animator moves a joint or exchanges a part between photographs. Only the selected poses enter the finished movement. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The opening puzzle: how does a cup of coffee become the moon?
visuals.title: Carry one visual feature across the cut
visuals.alt_text: A cup and a moon share a position and circular shape across a direct edit. The graphic relationship carries attention between otherwise different scenes.
visuals.caption: The circular shape holds attention across a direct cut. The cup and moon do not need to transform physically. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Several jobs hide under “wire work”
visuals.title: Separate support from the screen action
visuals.alt_text: Support above the frame helps a performer’s action while visible wires can later be removed. This conceptual separation specifies no engineering dimensions or operating procedure.
visuals.caption: The performer supplies the action while a support changes what movement is possible. Framing and cleanup conceal the assistance. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Rear projection: put the projector behind the screen
visuals.title: Put the image behind the performers
visuals.alt_text: An overhead plan places a translucent screen between a projector and the filming camera, with a performer on the camera side. The projected background and foreground are photographed together.
visuals.caption: The camera records the performer and a background transmitted through the screen. The projector stays behind the screen. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Front projection: send the image from the camera side
visuals.title: Return the background toward the camera
visuals.alt_text: An overhead plan shows a beam splitter aligning projection with the filming axis. A reflective screen returns the background toward the camera; practical systems also manage shadows and spill.
visuals.caption: A beam splitter aligns the projected image with the filming direction. The reflective screen returns the background toward the lens. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Example: *Nope* (2022)—how can we peer deep into the nighttime desert?
visuals.title: Give the night image usable ingredients
visuals.alt_text: Useful captured detail is shaped into a night image through exposure choices, sky treatment and local lighting. The two invented frames compare roles rather than claim a film-specific color grade.
visuals.caption: Preserve useful captured detail, then change the daylight cues separately. Darkening the whole image equally can leave it looking like daytime. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The puzzle: where is the water?
visuals.title: Make several underwater cues agree
visuals.alt_text: A performance, the behavior of hair and light, and added water detail contribute different underwater cues. The diagram separates those roles; it does not show a practical underwater rig.
visuals.caption: Suspension supplies floating, while movement, light and added detail suggest water. Every cue must describe the same underwater environment. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The classic trick: give the cloud somewhere to spread
visuals.title: Let a plume spread along a boundary
visuals.alt_text: A tank cutaway reveals two water layers of different density. A plume spreads near their boundary in one classic cloud-tank arrangement.
visuals.caption: A density boundary encourages a plume to spread instead of simply falling. Lighting and the final composite turn that motion into apparent sky. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: What do the terms mean?
visuals.title: Choose what moves with the set
visuals.alt_text: The set moves on a support while the camera either remains separate or rides with it. Relative movement changes the apparent horizon and the way the audience reads the action.
visuals.caption: A camera riding with the set keeps nearby scenery steadier. An independent camera sees the set tilt; the exterior horizon must agree with the intended journey. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The puzzle: why can heavy rain almost disappear on camera?
visuals.title: Make transparent rain visible
visuals.alt_text: Backlight helps transparent drops separate from a darker background. The drawing represents that photographic relationship without calculating scattering or rainfall density.
visuals.caption: Backlight helps transparent drops stand out against a darker background. Wetness alone does not guarantee visible screen rain. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The crowd needs direction at two scales
visuals.title: Direct the population at two scales
visuals.alt_text: Bodies, actions and local rules feed directed routes and density. Individual variation works within a designed population; important actions can still receive separate animation.
visuals.caption: Shared actions create individuals; routes, timing and density organize the crowd. Variation alone does not supply a readable collective purpose. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: What actually gets captured?
visuals.title: Preserve acting through a transformation
visuals.alt_text: Recorded acting is retargeted and refined for a character with different anatomy. The figures separate the input performance from the animation decisions that shape the result.
visuals.caption: Captured acting is adapted to another anatomy, then refined. Different proportions can change the meaning or contact of a copied movement. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The next puzzle: where does the appliance end?
visuals.title: Build volume and hide the join
visuals.alt_text: Added material provides central volume and tapers toward the actor’s skin. The enlarged section explains the join without specifying a particular appliance or application process.
visuals.caption: Added material changes the face’s volume. A thin, textured edge helps that material meet the actor’s skin without announcing the join. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: A face, a head, or an entire person?
visuals.title: Choose the extent of the replacement
visuals.alt_text: Green identifies a face region, whole head or complete body replacement. The remaining photography still needs coherent tracking, lighting, deformation and foreground overlap.
visuals.caption: Replace only the face, the head or the full body according to the shot. The new part must still share the photographed movement and light. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Three layers have to cooperate
visuals.title: Turn a control into visible behavior
visuals.alt_text: A cutaway of an invented creature head reveals a control input, an internal mechanism and a jaw pivot. The moving mechanism must carry the outer surface convincingly.
visuals.caption: A control moves the jaw mechanism, which must carry the outer skin convincingly. Coordinated operation turns mechanical motion into acting. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: How the transformation works
visuals.title: Design around the performing body
visuals.alt_text: A human figure inside an invented silhouette shows how joints and balance constrain a creature performance. Different shots may use another suit, head or puppet.
visuals.caption: The invented outline still contains a performer’s joints and balance. Design and movement must work together through the poses the scene needs. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The puzzle: when something disappears, what fills the hole?
visuals.title: Replace the missing pixels
visuals.alt_text: Removing the person requires reconstructed background imagery. Foreground overlap is restored after the repair; the marked repair region is shown for explanation and should disappear in a finished composite.
visuals.caption: Removal requires a new background, not just an empty cutout. Restore foreground overlaps so the repaired area remains behind the right objects. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The puzzle: how do you cut something out when it never stops changing?
visuals.title: A moving shape controls a layer
visuals.alt_text: A moving boundary follows an invented performer and selects the foreground layer. Green marks the selected region; it is a teaching color rather than the literal values of a grayscale alpha image.
visuals.caption: The changing boundary selects which layer appears. Green indicates the selected region here; an actual matte commonly uses grayscale values. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The puzzle: who animated every drop and piece of debris?
visuals.title: Advance a state, evaluate the result, then render
visuals.alt_text: A model combines state with forces and constraints, advances a time step and repeats. Artists review the motion before rendering; the falling points do not stand for a universal solver.
visuals.caption: Each small calculation advances the material’s motion. Artists direct and review those consequences before lighting and rendering the final image. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The basic trick: correspondence, warping, blending
visuals.title: Move corresponding features while blending appearance
visuals.alt_text: Corresponding eyes, mouth and silhouette move toward intermediate positions while the appearance blends. The invented faces explain landmark movement without warping film imagery.
visuals.caption: Corresponding features move while appearances blend. That gives the viewer a continuous relationship to follow through the change. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: The camera leaves clues
visuals.title: Recover the viewpoint from changes in the picture
visuals.alt_text: One camera occupies two successive positions beside fixed near and far points. Matching frame insets show the nearer feature shifting farther across the image.
visuals.caption: As one camera moves sideways, near details shift more than distant ones. The paired views show the evidence used to reconstruct its motion. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: How flat pictures reveal depth
visuals.title: Overlapping views constrain a shared surface point
visuals.alt_text: Two observations constrain a shared surface detail along viewing rays. A complete reconstruction uses many overlapping views and also estimates calibrated camera relationships.
visuals.caption: Overlapping views constrain where a shared feature sits in space. A complete reconstruction needs many such observations and camera relationships. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: Make the light agree with the event
visuals.title: Photograph the illumination before adding the fictional source
visuals.alt_text: A practical light supplies a photographed response on a real performer before the fictional source is completed. Light direction, intensity, color and timing must agree with the intended event.
visuals.caption: Photograph the invented source’s influence on real surfaces. The finished effect inherits those changing highlights, shadows and reflections. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.

visuals.anchor: A photograph that becomes a light source
visuals.title: Preserve brightness relationships and use them for illumination
visuals.alt_text: Short, medium and long exposure times contribute different brightness ranges to an HDR light map. Matte and reflective surfaces respond to that environment.
visuals.caption: Short exposures retain bright sources; long exposures record dark surroundings. Their combined brightness relationships can light a digital object. Illustrative scenario, not a documented film setup.
